corrected_finding.problem: Two problems in one card. First, the differential a resident is handed for the febrile, rigid, altered patient contains only drug syndromes — CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) and heat stroke are absent (the page's only nod to infection is 'clarify ... infection/medical triggers' in the collateral-stage narration, which is history-gathering, not a rule-out), and anchoring on NMS in a febrile patient on an antipsychotic without excluding meningitis delays antibiotics in the one item on the list that kills within hours — a dangerous omission from a rule-out list, hence S1. corrected_finding.replacement:
- Anticholinergic toxicity (dry skin, flushing, urinary retention, **absent** bowel sounds — the mirror image of serotonin syndrome's diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel)
- CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) and heat stroke — fever + rigidity + altered mentation is not NMS until these are excluded
corrected_finding.basis: Standard toxidrome differentiation (Boyer & Shannon NEJM 2005 for the serotonin syndrome/anticholinergic contrast); NMS is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring CNS infection to be ruled out before it is settled on.

reasoning: Quote is exact (line 1657) and the central number is wrong, now on better footing than the finding's 'low' confidence allowed. According to PubMed, Bot et al., 'The Effect of Benzodiazepines on Catatonia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', Acta Psychiatr Scand 2026;154(2):99-115 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/acps.70102)) — a paper already carried in this repo's own evidence list — reports overall response 77% and remission 55% across 53 studies; the older Hawkins et al. review (Int J Psychiatry Med 1995, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2190/X0FF-VU7G-QQP7-L5V7)) reports benzodiazepines effective in 70%, lorazepam 79% complete response, ECT 85%. So '~90%' overstates and the finding's 60–80% band is right. Three corrections. (1) The ECT sub-claim does not survive: published ECT response in catatonia spans roughly 59–100% across series (85% in Hawkins), so the page's '60–100%' is a defensible range rather than an error — drop that half. (2) The harm framing is overstated: the very next bullet already says ECT is 'first-line for malignant catatonia or benzodiazepine non-response', so the resident is not left without the ECT trigger. (3) The replacement's directive contradicts itself — 'treat a partial or absent response as the trigger to move to ECT rather than as a reason to keep climbing' sits in the same sentence as 'titrate to a standing regimen, often up to ~16 mg/day', and read literally would tell a resident to abandon titration at the first partial response; the correct teaching is titrate to an adequate trial, then move to ECT for inadequate response, and to ECT immediately in malignant catatonia. Worth adding: no entry in evidence_annotations.json covers this figure, so '~90%' is also an untraceable statistic under this review's own rule. Heckers & Walther NEJM 2023 has no abstract in PubMed and no PMC full text, so it could not be used to settle anything — basis re-anchored to Bot 2026 and Hawkins 1995, and confidence raised low → high.

corrected_finding.quote: - Effective in ~90%; titrate to a standing regimen, often up to ~16 mg/day (higher only under close monitoring).
corrected_finding.problem: Benzodiazepine response in catatonia is reported at roughly 60–80%, not ~90%: the 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis found 77% response and only 55% remission, and the classic review reports 70% for benzodiazepines overall / 79% complete response for lorazepam. On a numbers page for residents the inflated figure makes a partial or absent response look like an anomaly to be titrated through rather than the expected minority outcome that should start the ECT conversation. The figure is also untraceable — no evidence annotation in the repo covers it. (The neighbouring ECT figure of 60–100% is a defensible published range and is not part of this finding.)
corrected_finding.replacement: - Response is generally reported at roughly **60–80%** (2026 meta-analysis: 77% response, 55% full remission) — good, but not near-universal; titrate to an adequate standing regimen, often up to ~16 mg/day (higher only under close monitoring), and when the response is still partial or absent after an adequate trial, move to ECT rather than continuing to climb — immediately in malignant catatonia.
corrected_finding.basis: Bot L, Schotsman B, Oostra E, et al. The Effect of Benzodiazepines on Catatonia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Acta Psychiatr Scand. 2026;154(2):99-115. doi:10.1111/acps.70102 (53 studies; response 77%, remission 55%) — already listed in this library's own evidence page. Corroborated by Hawkins JM, et al. Somatic treatment of catatonia. Int J Psychiatry Med. 1995;25(4):345-69 (benzodiazepines effective 70%, lorazepam 79% complete response, ECT 85%). Heckers & Walther, NEJM 2023, carries no retrievable abstract and was not used.

Among adults with a history of self-harm it may be an effective intervention.' The tool string therefore teaches a stratum result as the trial's unconditional effect — exactly the failure mode the repo's evidence policy names. One nuance that strengthens rather than weakens the finding: the first-presentation and repeat-presentation comparisons were a priori primary outcomes, so this is a pre-specified stratum, not a post-hoc trawl; the proposed replacement does not mis-state that and is accurate as written. Severity S2 ('a trial result mis-summarised') is right; the stated confidence can now be raised from low to high.
